Question 1 of 20
  1. 1

    For the relation x=y3−yx = y^3 - yx=y3−y, which statement is correct?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Assumes the first coordinate is always the input, so it reports the verdict for the wrong variable.

    You chose C: Checks only that each yyy produces one xxx and never runs the reading in the other direction, and assumes the other reading must behave the same way.

    You chose D: Takes a relation that fails one reading to fail the other reading as well.

    Nothing in a set of points names the input, so test both readings. With yyy as the input the rule hands back the single number y3−yy^3 - yy3−y, one output every time. With xxx as the input, ask which values of yyy sit above x=0x = 0x=0.

    y3−y=y(y−1)(y+1)=0⟹y=−1, 0, 1y^3 - y = y(y - 1)(y + 1) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y = -1,\ 0,\ 1y3−y=y(y−1)(y+1)=0⟹y=−1, 0, 1

    Three outputs for the one input 000, so with xxx as the input it is not a function.

  2. 2

    Let f(x)=5−x2f(x) = 5 - x^2f(x)=5−x2. Which expression equals f(3t)f(3t)f(3t)?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Squares only the ttt, leaving the coefficient 333 outside the square.

    You chose B: Computes 3f(t)3f(t)3f(t), scaling the output instead of the input.

    You chose D: Squares the input correctly but subtracts in the wrong order, negating the whole rule.

    The argument is a slot: whatever sits inside is copied into every xxx of the rule, coefficient included, and then squared.

    f(3t)=5−(3t)2=5−9t2f(3t) = 5 - (3t)^2 = 5 - 9t^2f(3t)=5−(3t)2=5−9t2

    The 333 is inside the slot, so it is squared along with ttt.

  3. 3

    What is the natural domain of f(x)=x+6x2−4xf(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 6}}{x^2 - 4x}f(x)=x2−4xx+6​​?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Clears the denominator but never requires the inside of the square root to be nonnegative.

    You chose B: Solves x2=4xx^2 = 4xx2=4x by dividing both sides by xxx, which loses the excluded input x=0x = 0x=0.

    You chose C: Makes the radical condition strict, as though the square root sat in the denominator.

    Two requirements must hold at once, and the domain is their overlap, not either one alone. The square root needs a nonnegative inside, and the denominator factors as x(x−4)x(x - 4)x(x−4).

    x+6≥0andx(x−4)≠0x + 6 \ge 0 \quad\text{and}\quad x(x - 4) \ne 0x+6≥0andx(x−4)=0

    So the domain is x≥−6x \ge -6x≥−6 with x=0x = 0x=0 and x=4x = 4x=4 removed. The root sits on top, so its inside is allowed to be zero.

  4. 4

    What is the sign of f(x)=(x+5)(x−1)(x−8)f(x) = (x + 5)(x - 1)(x - 8)f(x)=(x+5)(x−1)(x−8) on the interval −5<x<1-5 < x < 1−5<x<1?

    Answer choices for question 4

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Counts the single positive factor against the two negative ones and reads the product as negative.

    You chose C: Confuses the interval between two consecutive roots with the roots themselves.

    You chose D: Expects a sign change between consecutive roots rather than at them.

    No factor has a root inside the interval, so no factor changes sign across it: read each factor's fixed sign there and multiply. On −5<x<1-5 < x < 1−5<x<1 the first factor is positive and the other two are negative.

    (+)(−)(−)=+(+)(-)(-) = +(+)(−)(−)=+

    Two negatives make a positive, so f>0f > 0f>0 throughout the interval.

  5. 5

    Let f(x)=x−7f(x) = x - 7f(x)=x−7 and g(x)=x2g(x) = x^2g(x)=x2. Which expression equals (g∘f)(x)(g \circ f)(x)(g∘f)(x)?

    Answer choices for question 5

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Runs the composition in the other order, computing (f∘g)(x)=x2−7(f \circ g)(x) = x^2 - 7(f∘g)(x)=x2−7.

    You chose C: Squares each term of x−7x - 7x−7 separately instead of expanding the square.

    You chose D: Expands the square but takes (−7)2(-7)^2(−7)2 as −49-49−49.

    In g∘fg \circ fg∘f the function on the right acts first, so fff sends xxx to x−7x - 7x−7 and ggg squares that whole result.

    (g∘f)(x)=g(x−7)=(x−7)2=x2−14x+49(g \circ f)(x) = g(x - 7) = (x - 7)^2 = x^2 - 14x + 49(g∘f)(x)=g(x−7)=(x−7)2=x2−14x+49

    The cross term −14x-14x−14x is what separates a squared binomial from a term-by-term square.

    The point (−3,7)(-3, 7)(−3,7) lies on the graph of y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x). Where does it land on the graph of y=f(x+2)−5y = f(x + 2) - 5y=f(x+2)−5?

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads the inside +2+2+2 as a move to the right, shifting the input the way the sign is written.

    You chose B: Handles the inside correctly but adds the outside 555 to the height instead of subtracting it.

    You chose D: Uses the inside sign directly, moving the input right 222, and then reverses the sign of the outside constant, raising the height by 555 instead of lowering it.

    Match the shape y=a f(b(x−h))+ky = a\,f\big(b(x - h)\big) + ky=af(b(x−h))+k: here b=1b = 1b=1, h=−2h = -2h=−2, a=1a = 1a=1 and k=−5k = -5k=−5. A point (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) on fff lands at (ub+h, av+k)\left(\tfrac{u}{b} + h,\ av + k\right)(bu​+h, av+k).

    (−3, 7)⟼(−3−2, 7−5)=(−5, 2)(-3,\ 7) \longmapsto (-3 - 2,\ 7 - 5) = (-5,\ 2)(−3, 7)⟼(−3−2, 7−5)=(−5, 2)

    The inside acts on the number handed to fff, so finding the new input means solving x+2=−3x + 2 = -3x+2=−3, which moves the point left.

  7. 7

    On all real numbers, is f(x)=2x6−x3f(x) = 2x^6 - x^3f(x)=2x6−x3 even, odd, or neither?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Reads the parity off the leading exponent alone instead of computing f(−x)f(-x)f(−x).

    You chose C: Classifies from the one term that flips, ignoring that the x6x^6x6 term does not.

    You chose D: Awards the function each identity because one of its two terms satisfies each.

    The domain is all real numbers, which is symmetric about 000, so the question can be asked at all. Substitute −x-x−x and compare with both targets.

    f(−x)=2(−x)6−(−x)3=2x6+x3f(-x) = 2(-x)^6 - (-x)^3 = 2x^6 + x^3f(−x)=2(−x)6−(−x)3=2x6+x3

    That is neither f(x)=2x6−x3f(x) = 2x^6 - x^3f(x)=2x6−x3 nor −f(x)=−2x6+x3-f(x) = -2x^6 + x^3−f(x)=−2x6+x3, so fff is neither. Mixed exponent parity is exactly where the exponent shortcut fails.

    Let f(x)=3xx+5f(x) = \dfrac{3x}{x + 5}f(x)=x+53x​ on x≠−5x \ne -5x=−5, with its codomain taken to be its range. What is f−1f^{-1}f−1?

    Answer choices for question 8

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Gathers the xxx terms but drops the minus sign at the division, reversing the denominator.

    You chose C: Turns the fraction upside down, reading f−1f^{-1}f−1 as the reciprocal 1f\tfrac{1}{f}f1​.

    You chose D: Negates the constant inside the rule, as if inverting meant flipping the sign of 555.

    Write y=3xx+5y = \dfrac{3x}{x + 5}y=x+53x​ and solve for the input: clear the denominator, gather the xxx terms, factor, then divide.

    y(x+5)=3x ⟹ x(y−3)=−5y ⟹ x=5y3−yy(x + 5) = 3x \ \Longrightarrow\ x(y - 3) = -5y \ \Longrightarrow\ x = \frac{5y}{3 - y}y(x+5)=3x ⟹ x(y−3)=−5y ⟹ x=3−y5y​

    Renaming the input gives f−1(x)=5x3−xf^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{5x}{3 - x}f−1(x)=3−x5x​, and its excluded input 333 is exactly the one value fff never outputs.

    For f(x)=4−3x2f(x) = 4 - 3x^2f(x)=4−3x2, which statement about f(x+h)−f(x)h\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}hf(x+h)−f(x)​ is correct?

    Answer choices for question 9

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Distributes the −3-3−3 across (x+h)2(x + h)^2(x+h)2 but flips the sign on the h2h^2h2 term, leaving −6xh+3h2h\dfrac{-6xh + 3h^2}{h}h−6xh+3h2​.

    You chose B: Sets h=0h = 0h=0 in the simplified form, the one input the quotient itself forbids.

    You chose C: Lets the cancelled hhh widen the domain, forgetting that the left-hand side has no value at all when h=0h = 0h=0.

    Expand, subtract, and check that every surviving term carries a factor of hhh before dividing.

    (4−3(x+h)2)−(4−3x2)h=−6xh−3h2h=−6x−3h,h≠0\frac{\big(4 - 3(x + h)^2\big) - \big(4 - 3x^2\big)}{h} = \frac{-6xh - 3h^2}{h} = -6x - 3h, \qquad h \ne 0h(4−3(x+h)2)−(4−3x2)​=h−6xh−3h2​=−6x−3h,h=0

    Cancelling the hhh is a division, so the identity is claimed only where h≠0h \ne 0h=0: at h=0h = 0h=0 the quotient reads 00\tfrac{0}{0}00​ and returns nothing for the simplified form to match.

  10. 10

    The graph of f(x)=(x+2)4(x−5)f(x) = (x + 2)^4(x - 5)f(x)=(x+2)4(x−5) meets the horizontal axis at two inputs. What does it do at each?

    Answer choices for question 10

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Treats every zero as a crossing, reading the root rather than the power on its factor.

    You chose B: Swaps the two verdicts, attaching the touching to the second factor written rather than to the one carrying the even power.

    You chose D: Lets the fourth power govern the whole product, leaving no factor to flip the sign.

    A factor raised to an even power is a square, so it is never negative and holds one sign on both sides of its root; an odd power carries the sign of the single factor and flips.

    (x+2)4>0 for every x≠−2,(x−5) changes sign at 5(x + 2)^4 > 0 \text{ for every } x \ne -2, \qquad (x - 5) \text{ changes sign at } 5(x+2)4>0 for every x=−2,(x−5) changes sign at 5

    So the sign of fff is unchanged across −2-2−2, where the graph meets the axis and turns back, and flips across 555, where it crosses.

  11. 11

    The graph of f(x)=x2−6x+5x2−8x+15f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 6x + 5}{x^2 - 8x + 15}f(x)=x2−8x+15x2−6x+5​ is missing exactly one point. Which point?

    Answer choices for question 11

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Takes the height of the missing point from the numerator's zero, reading the cancelled input as an output of 000.

    You chose C: Reports the two excluded inputs as the coordinates of one point instead of testing which factor cancels.

    You chose D: Uses the numerator zero that does not cancel, which is an ordinary horizontal-axis crossing rather than a gap.

    Factor both parts and keep track of which excluded input survives the cancelling.

    f(x)=(x−1)(x−5)(x−3)(x−5)=x−1x−3,x≠5f(x) = \frac{(x - 1)(x - 5)}{(x - 3)(x - 5)} = \frac{x - 1}{x - 3}, \qquad x \ne 5f(x)=(x−3)(x−5)(x−1)(x−5)​=x−3x−1​,x=5

    The input 333 does not cancel, so the graph runs off along a vertical line there rather than losing a single point. The input 555 does cancel, so evaluating the simplified rule gives the gap's height, 5−15−3=2\tfrac{5 - 1}{5 - 3} = 25−35−1​=2.

  12. 12

    A graph of y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) passes through (8,−1)(8, -1)(8,−1). At which input does that same height appear on the graph of y=f(4x−12)y = f(4x - 12)y=f(4x−12)?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Reads the shift straight off the −12-12−12 without pulling out the factor 444 first.

    You chose B: Feeds the old input into the inside, computing 4(8)−124(8) - 124(8)−12 instead of solving for xxx.

    You chose C: Divides by 444 but then subtracts the shift instead of adding it.

    Factor the inside so the compression and the shift are both visible, then solve for the input that makes the inside equal the old input 888.

    4x−12=4(x−3),4x−12=8 ⟹ x=84+3=54x - 12 = 4(x - 3), \qquad 4x - 12 = 8 \ \Longrightarrow\ x = \frac{8}{4} + 3 = 54x−12=4(x−3),4x−12=8 ⟹ x=48​+3=5

    The shift is 333, not 121212: the factor 444 divides it, so it has to come out before any shift can be read.

  13. 13

    A relation passes the horizontal line test and fails the vertical line test. Which statement is correct?

    Answer choices for question 13

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads the horizontal line test as certifying xxx as the input, when it certifies yyy.

    You chose B: Lets one failed test settle both readings, though each test speaks about one reading only.

    You chose D: Reads one-to-oneness off the same test that made the yyy reading a function, when it is the vertical test that decides it.

    Each test speaks about one reading, and one-to-oneness of a reading is settled by the OTHER test. The horizontal test asks whether yyy can be the input; the vertical test asks whether xxx can.

    horizontal passes⇒y is a legal input,vertical fails⇒x is not\text{horizontal passes} \Rightarrow y \text{ is a legal input}, \qquad \text{vertical fails} \Rightarrow x \text{ is not}horizontal passes⇒y is a legal input,vertical fails⇒x is not

    Since the vertical test fails, some value of xxx carries two points, so two different yyy inputs share one output and the reading that works repeats a value. One-to-oneness of a reading is a second question, answered by the test the first question did not use.

  14. 14

    Let f(x)=x+3f(x) = \sqrt{x + 3}f(x)=x+3​ and g(x)=1x−6g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 6}g(x)=x−61​. What is the domain of g∘fg \circ fg∘f?

    Answer choices for question 14

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Intersects the two domains, removing the input ggg rejects instead of the input whose image lands there.

    You chose C: Stops at what fff accepts and never asks whether the output of fff is legal for ggg.

    You chose D: Imposes the second condition but drops the requirement that fff accept the input at all.

    Two things must be true: fff must accept xxx, and ggg must accept the number f(x)f(x)f(x) that comes out.

    x+3≥0andx+3≠6 ⟹ x+3≠36x + 3 \ge 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \sqrt{x + 3} \ne 6 \ \Longrightarrow\ x + 3 \ne 36x+3≥0andx+3​=6 ⟹ x+3=36

    So the domain is x≥−3x \ge -3x≥−3 with x=33x = 33x=33 removed. The excluded input is found through the values fff actually produces, not by intersecting the two domains.

  15. 15

    Let p(x)=3x4−8xp(x) = 3x^4 - 8xp(x)=3x4−8x. How do the two ends of the graph of y=−p(x)+7y = -p(x) + 7y=−p(x)+7 behave?

    Answer choices for question 15

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Reads the ends off ppp and forgets that the outside factor −1-1−1 reflects every height.

    You chose C: Treats the degree as odd, letting the −8x-8x−8x term govern the ends.

    You chose D: Reads the outside +7+7+7 as a ceiling the transformed graph settles onto.

    Settle the ends of ppp first by factoring out the highest power, then apply the outside map to the heights.

    p(x)=x4(3−8x3),∣8x3∣≤1 once ∣x∣≥2p(x) = x^4\left(3 - \frac{8}{x^3}\right), \qquad \left\lvert \frac{8}{x^3} \right\rvert \le 1 \text{ once } \lvert x \rvert \ge 2p(x)=x4(3−x38​),​x38​​≤1 once ∣x∣≥2

    The bracket stays positive and x4x^4x4 is never negative, so both ends of ppp climb without bound. The outside map sends a height vvv to −v+7-v + 7−v+7, which negates it, so both ends of the transformed graph fall without bound; adding 777 raises them but cannot stop them.

  16. 16

    For f(x)=4x2−xf(x) = 4x^2 - xf(x)=4x2−x, which expression equals f(a+b)−f(a)−f(b)f(a + b) - f(a) - f(b)f(a+b)−f(a)−f(b)?

    Answer choices for question 16

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Expands (a+b)2(a + b)^2(a+b)2 as a2+ab+b2a^2 + ab + b^2a2+ab+b2, halving the cross term.

    You chose B: Assumes every polynomial rule is additive, so the difference has to vanish.

    You chose C: Writes f(a)+f(b)f(a) + f(b)f(a)+f(b) as 4a2+a+4b2+b4a^2 + a + 4b^2 + b4a2+a+4b2+b, flipping the sign of both linear terms.

    Put the whole sum into the slot, then subtract the two separate outputs.

    (4a2+8ab+4b2−a−b)−(4a2−a)−(4b2−b)=8ab\big(4a^2 + 8ab + 4b^2 - a - b\big) - \big(4a^2 - a\big) - \big(4b^2 - b\big) = 8ab(4a2+8ab+4b2−a−b)−(4a2−a)−(4b2−b)=8ab

    The squared term leaves the cross term 8ab8ab8ab behind while the linear term cancels exactly, which is why a rule carrying a squared term can never be additive.

  17. 17

    No inverse exists for f(x)=(x+7)2f(x) = (x + 7)^2f(x)=(x+7)2 on the whole real line. One student keeps only the inputs x≥−7x \ge -7x≥−7, and another keeps only x≤−7x \le -7x≤−7. Which statement is correct?

    Answer choices for question 17

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Treats the convention that x\sqrt{\phantom{x}}x​ means the nonnegative root as ruling out the other restriction.

    You chose C: Applies the uniqueness theorem across two different functions instead of within one.

    You chose D: Overlooks that each cut removes one member of every pair that shared an output.

    Restricting a domain does not repair fff; it replaces fff with a different function, and each of these two is one-to-one, so each earns its own inverse.

    y=(x+7)2 ⟹ x=−7+y  (x≥−7),x=−7−y  (x≤−7)y = (x + 7)^2 \ \Longrightarrow\ x = -7 + \sqrt{y}\ \ (x \ge -7), \qquad x = -7 - \sqrt{y}\ \ (x \le -7)y=(x+7)2 ⟹ x=−7+y​  (x≥−7),x=−7−y​  (x≤−7)

    Uniqueness says one function has at most one inverse. These are two different functions, so two different answers are exactly what should appear.

  18. 18

    Which statement about f(x)=x5−9x3f(x) = x^5 - 9x^3f(x)=x5−9x3 on all real numbers is correct?

    Answer choices for question 18

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads x2−9x^2 - 9x2−9 as having no real root, as though it were x2+9x^2 + 9x2+9, then classifies the parity from that even cofactor alone, ignoring the outer x3x^3x3.

    You chose B: Tests parity by comparing coefficients rather than by computing f(−x)f(-x)f(−x).

    You chose D: Reads the multiplicity 333 at the origin as an even power because the graph flattens there.

    Factor first, then test the parity by substituting −x-x−x.

    f(x)=x3(x−3)(x+3),f(−x)=−x5+9x3=−f(x)f(x) = x^3(x - 3)(x + 3), \qquad f(-x) = -x^5 + 9x^3 = -f(x)f(x)=x3(x−3)(x+3),f(−x)=−x5+9x3=−f(x)

    So fff is odd on its symmetric domain. Every factor carries an odd power, 333, 111 and 111, so the sign flips at each of −3-3−3, 000 and 333 and the graph crosses at all three.

  19. 19

    Two moves act on the input of fff: a horizontal compression by 333, which divides every input by 333, and a shift right 666. Which rule applies the compression first and the shift second?

    Answer choices for question 19

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Reaches the factored inside 3(x−6)3(x - 6)3(x−6) and then clears the bracket by dividing the shift by 333 instead of multiplying it.

    You chose B: Writes a shift to the right as an addition inside, ignoring that the inside runs against its sign.

    You chose C: Writes the compression as dividing xxx by 333, which stretches the graph instead of compressing it, and then appends the shift at the end rather than substituting it through the inside already there.

    Compressing sends an input uuu to u3\tfrac{u}{3}3u​, and shifting right then sends that to u3+6\tfrac{u}{3} + 63u​+6. Matching the landing rule ub+h\tfrac{u}{b} + hbu​+h reads off b=3b = 3b=3 and h=6h = 6h=6.

    y=f(3(x−6))=f(3x−18)y = f\big(3(x - 6)\big) = f(3x - 18)y=f(3(x−6))=f(3x−18)

    Composing the same two maps the other way round sends uuu to u+63=u3+2\tfrac{u + 6}{3} = \tfrac{u}{3} + 23u+6​=3u​+2, a different landing at every input. The two maps do not commute, so the order is part of the answer.

  20. 20

    A rule fff satisfies f(x+2)=3x−5f(x + 2) = 3x - 5f(x+2)=3x−5 for every real number xxx. What is f(x)f(x)f(x)?

    Answer choices for question 20

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Reads the given equation as the rule itself, ignoring that the slot holds x+2x + 2x+2 rather than xxx.

    You chose C: Substitutes x+2x + 2x+2 into the right-hand side instead of solving for what the slot receives.

    You chose D: Subtracts the 222 once at the end rather than passing it through the factor 333.

    The equation says what fff does to the number x+2x + 2x+2, so name that number and re-express the right side in terms of it. Put u=x+2u = x + 2u=x+2, so that x=u−2x = u - 2x=u−2.

    f(u)=3(u−2)−5=3u−11f(u) = 3(u - 2) - 5 = 3u - 11f(u)=3(u−2)−5=3u−11

    Renaming the input gives f(x)=3x−11f(x) = 3x - 11f(x)=3x−11, and the check runs forward: f(x+2)=3(x+2)−11=3x−5f(x + 2) = 3(x + 2) - 11 = 3x - 5f(x+2)=3(x+2)−11=3x−5.

Review: Function Notation and Evaluation

  • Classify a rule as even, odd or neither on a domain symmetric about 000, arguing from f(−x)f(-x)f(−x) rather than from a glance at the exponents. Review: Graphs of Functions , Transformations of Graphs
  • Locate the point an excluded input removes from a graph, and tell a cancelling factor apart from one that survives. Review: Graphs of Functions
  • Transform a point, a domain or a range under y=a f(b(x−h))+ky = a\,f(b(x-h)) + ky=af(b(x−h))+k, factoring a compound inside before reading any shift, and keeping the order of two moves on the same side. Review: Transformations of Graphs
  • Compose and decompose: which function acts first, the domain of a composite, whether a particular pair commutes, and a superscript on a function name as counting compositions. Review: Composition of Functions
  • Establish invertibility rather than assume it: the two-sided test, one-to-oneness with the codomain taken to be the range, a domain restriction as a choice, and the swap of coordinates behind the mirror in y=xy = xy=x. Review: Inverse Functions

    1. One curve, and a question that waits on a declaration . 9 points. Question 1 of 10.

    9 pts

    The relation x=y2−4yx = y^2 - 4yx=y2−4y is a set of points in the plane. Each part below declares which coordinate is fed in.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Declare yyy to be the input and state the rule that produces the output. Then declare xxx to be the input, solve for yyy, and report every output the input x=5x = 5x=5 receives.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Declare yyy to be the input again and decide whether that function is one-to-one. Name two inputs that settle it, and say what the verdict predicts about the reading with xxx as the input.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate insists that 'is this curve a function' can be settled by looking at the curve alone, with nothing further supplied. Identify the part of that position which is sound, and the precise step at which it fails. Then say how the vertical line test and the horizontal line test are related to the two readings.

      Carry your own answer forward Argue from the two readings your own earlier work produced, expected or not. The credit here is for locating the verdict in the pairing of a curve with a declared input, not for reproducing one particular answer.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    With yyy as the input the rule is x=y2−4yx = y^2 - 4yx=y2−4y, one output for each input. With xxx as the input, y=2±x+4y = 2 \pm \sqrt{x + 4}y=2±x+4​, so x=5x = 5x=5 receives the two outputs y=5y = 5y=5 and y=−1y = -1y=−1.

    Part B

    It is not one-to-one: the inputs y=0y = 0y=0 and y=4y = 4y=4 both produce x=0x = 0x=0. Two inputs sharing an output is exactly what makes the reversed reading fail, so with xxx as the input the relation cannot be a function.

    Part C

    Right that the set of points is fixed. What is not fixed is which coordinate is fed in, so the verdict belongs to the curve together with a declared input: this curve is a function of yyy and not of xxx. The two line tests are one test asked about the two readings, the vertical one about xxx and the horizontal one about yyy.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    With yyy declared the input, the relation already reads as a rule: square the input, subtract four times it, and hand back the single number that results. One output every time.

    With xxx declared the input, the output yyy has to be dug out, so complete the square.

    y2−4y−x=0 ⟹ (y−2)2=x+4 ⟹ y=2±x+4y^2 - 4y - x = 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ (y - 2)^2 = x + 4 \ \Longrightarrow\ y = 2 \pm \sqrt{x + 4}y2−4y−x=0 ⟹ (y−2)2=x+4 ⟹ y=2±x+4​

    At x=5x = 5x=5 this gives y=2±3y = 2 \pm 3y=2±3, the two outputs 555 and −1-1−1. Both check against the original relation, since 52−4(5)=55^2 - 4(5) = 552−4(5)=5 and (−1)2−4(−1)=5(-1)^2 - 4(-1) = 5(−1)2−4(−1)=5. One input with two outputs is what a function forbids.

    Part B

    Write the yyy reading as g(y)=y2−4y=(y−2)2−4g(y) = y^2 - 4y = (y - 2)^2 - 4g(y)=y2−4y=(y−2)2−4, which takes the same value at inputs equally far either side of 222.

    g(0)=0=g(4)g(0) = 0 = g(4)g(0)=0=g(4)

    Two different inputs share the output 000, so ggg is not one-to-one. Now swap the coordinates of every pair, which is what changing the declaration does: those two pairs become (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) and (0,4)(0, 4)(0,4), which share a first coordinate. So the swapped reading is not a function, and the failure part A found at x=5x = 5x=5 is the same failure seen at x=0x = 0x=0.

    Part C

    What is right. The relation is one fixed set of points. Nothing about the picture changes when the question changes, and the classmate is right to resist the idea that a curve is somehow two objects.

    Where it breaks. Being a function is not a property of the set of points; it is a property of that set together with a choice of which coordinate is the input. The choice comes from outside the set, and the two choices give opposite answers here:

    y as input: one output eachx as input: x=5 gives y=5 and y=−1y \text{ as input: one output each} \qquad x \text{ as input: } x = 5 \text{ gives } y = 5 \text{ and } y = -1y as input: one output eachx as input: x=5 gives y=5 and y=−1

    So the honest form of the question is always 'a function of which variable', and the vertical line test is the answer for one reading while the horizontal line test is the answer for the other.

    In one line

    With yyy as the input the relation is a function, x=y2−4yx = y^2 - 4yx=y2−4y, but not a one-to-one one, since g(0)=g(4)=0g(0) = g(4) = 0g(0)=g(4)=0. With xxx as the input it is not a function at all: y=2±x+4y = 2 \pm \sqrt{x + 4}y=2±x+4​, so x=5x = 5x=5 carries the two outputs 555 and −1-1−1. 'Is this a function' therefore has no answer until the input variable is declared.

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate says the simplified fraction IS the difference quotient, on the grounds that the two agree everywhere the fraction is defined. Decide whether the two are the same expression, say what the classmate's position gets right, and justify your verdict from the equality test; if they are not the same, name an input that separates them.

      Carry your own answer forward Run the argument on whichever simplified form you produced in part A, and say honestly what your own cancelling step did to the inputs the expression accepts. The credit is for the account of what equality of expressions demands, not for a particular fraction.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    Simplifying gives the bare formula −3(x+1)(x+h+1)\dfrac{-3}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)}(x+1)(x+h+1)−3​; what represents the difference quotient is that formula restricted by h≠0h \ne 0h=0, carrying x≠−1x \ne -1x=−1 and x+h≠−1x + h \ne -1x+h=−1 as well.

    • −3(x+1)(x+h+1)-\dfrac{3}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)}−(x+1)(x+h+1)3​ is the same fraction with the sign written outside; what is not the same is an answer with no restrictions attached, since the restrictions are part of what the expression means

    Part B

    Both routes give −14-\tfrac{1}{4}−41​. It is the slope of the line through the two points of the graph at inputs 222 and 333, so the output falls by a quarter of a unit per unit of input across that step.

    Part C

    Right that the two agree wherever both are defined. But the bare formula, on its own natural domain, accepts h=0h = 0h=0, where the quotient reads 00\tfrac{0}{0}00​: equality needs the same domain, not matching values alone. What the quotient equals is that formula restricted by h≠0h \ne 0h=0.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Put the whole expression x+hx + hx+h into the slot, then combine the two fractions over a common denominator rather than expanding anything.

    3x+h+1−3x+1=3(x+1)−3(x+h+1)(x+1)(x+h+1)=−3h(x+1)(x+h+1)\frac{3}{x + h + 1} - \frac{3}{x + 1} = \frac{3(x + 1) - 3(x + h + 1)}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)} = \frac{-3h}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)}x+h+13​−x+13​=(x+1)(x+h+1)3(x+1)−3(x+h+1)​=(x+1)(x+h+1)−3h​

    Every surviving term carries a factor of hhh, which is the check that the subtraction was done correctly. Dividing by hhh cancels it:

    f(x+h)−f(x)h=−3(x+1)(x+h+1),h≠0.\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \frac{-3}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)}, \qquad h \ne 0.hf(x+h)−f(x)​=(x+1)(x+h+1)−3​,h=0.

    The restrictions x≠−1x \ne -1x=−1 and x+h≠−1x + h \ne -1x+h=−1 come from fff having to be defined at both inputs; h≠0h \ne 0h=0 comes from the division that produced the bare formula, and it is what separates that formula from the quotient it is standing in for.

    Part B

    From the simplified form, with x=2x = 2x=2 and h=1h = 1h=1:

    −3(2+1)(2+1+1)=−312=−14\frac{-3}{(2 + 1)(2 + 1 + 1)} = \frac{-3}{12} = -\frac{1}{4}(2+1)(2+1+1)−3​=12−3​=−41​

    Directly, f(3)=34f(3) = \tfrac{3}{4}f(3)=43​ and f(2)=1f(2) = 1f(2)=1, so the quotient is 34−1=−14\tfrac{3}{4} - 1 = -\tfrac{1}{4}43​−1=−41​. The two agree, as they must for h≠0h \ne 0h=0. The quantity is the secant slope from input 222 to input 333, the average rate of change of fff across that step, and it is negative because this rule falls as the input grows.

    Part C

    What is right. For every h≠0h \ne 0h=0 the two expressions produce the same number, and part B checked one such case.

    Where it breaks. The equality test demands the same domain, the same codomain and the same values, not values alone. At h=0h = 0h=0 the original quotient has a zero denominator and no value, while the bare formula, read on its own natural domain, is defined:

    f(x+h)−f(x)h∣h=0=00,−3(x+1)(x+h+1)∣h=0=−3(x+1)2\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}\bigg|_{h = 0} = \frac{0}{0}, \qquad \frac{-3}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)}\bigg|_{h = 0} = \frac{-3}{(x + 1)^2}hf(x+h)−f(x)​​h=0​=00​,(x+1)(x+h+1)−3​​h=0​=(x+1)2−3​

    So h=0h = 0h=0 is the input that separates them: it lies in one domain and not the other. The cancelling step is a division by hhh, and dividing is exactly what removed that input from the record. Attach the restriction h≠0h \ne 0h=0 to the formula and the two objects do coincide; leave it off and they do not.

    In one line

    f(x+h)−f(x)h=−3(x+1)(x+h+1)\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \dfrac{-3}{(x + 1)(x + h + 1)}hf(x+h)−f(x)​=(x+1)(x+h+1)−3​ for h≠0h \ne 0h=0, with x≠−1x \ne -1x=−1 and x+h≠−1x + h \ne -1x+h=−1. At x=2x = 2x=2, h=1h = 1h=1 both routes give −14-\tfrac{1}{4}−41​, the average rate of change from input 222 to input 333. Taken on its own natural domain, the bare formula is a different expression from the quotient, because it accepts h=0h = 0h=0 and the quotient does not; restricted by h≠0h \ne 0h=0, it is the quotient.

    The answer

    Part A

    Zeros at x=−6x = -6x=−6 and x=2x = 2x=2. f>0f > 0f>0 on x<−6x < -6x<−6 and on −6<x<2-6 < x < 2−6<x<2, and f<0f < 0f<0 on x>2x > 2x>2.

    Part B

    f(x)=x3(−1−10x−12x2+72x3)f(x) = x^3\left(-1 - \tfrac{10}{x} - \tfrac{12}{x^2} + \tfrac{72}{x^3}\right)f(x)=x3(−1−x10​−x212​+x372​). For ∣x∣≥24\lvert x \rvert \ge 24∣x∣≥24 the bracket is negative, so fff rises on the far left and falls on the far right.

    Part C

    At x=−6x = -6x=−6 the factor is squared, so it is never negative and the sign of fff is the same on both sides: the graph meets the axis and turns back. At x=2x = 2x=2 the factor (2−x)(2 - x)(2−x) carries the power 111, so the sign flips there and the graph crosses.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is, so the zeros are x=2x = 2x=2 from (2−x)(2 - x)(2−x) and x=−6x = -6x=−6 from (x+6)2(x + 6)^2(x+6)2. Those two cut the line into three intervals, and inside each one no factor changes sign.

    x<−6: (+)(+)=+,−6<x<2: (+)(+)=+,x>2: (−)(+)=−x < -6:\ (+)(+) = +, \qquad -6 < x < 2:\ (+)(+) = +, \qquad x > 2:\ (-)(+) = -x<−6: (+)(+)=+,−6<x<2: (+)(+)=+,x>2: (−)(+)=−

    The squared factor is positive away from −6-6−6 and contributes a +++ on both sides of it, so the only sign change comes from (2−x)(2 - x)(2−x), which turns negative once xxx passes 222.

    Part B

    Expand first, then pull out the highest power.

    f(x)=(2−x)(x2+12x+36)=−x3−10x2−12x+72=x3(−1−10x−12x2+72x3)f(x) = (2 - x)(x^2 + 12x + 36) = -x^3 - 10x^2 - 12x + 72 = x^3\left(-1 - \frac{10}{x} - \frac{12}{x^2} + \frac{72}{x^3}\right)f(x)=(2−x)(x2+12x+36)=−x3−10x2−12x+72=x3(−1−x10​−x212​+x372​)

    Now bound the correction terms. Once ∣x∣≥24\lvert x \rvert \ge 24∣x∣≥24 we have ∣10x∣≤512\left\lvert \tfrac{10}{x} \right\rvert \le \tfrac{5}{12}​x10​​≤125​, ∣12x2∣≤148\left\lvert \tfrac{12}{x^2} \right\rvert \le \tfrac{1}{48}​x212​​≤481​ and ∣72x3∣≤1192\left\lvert \tfrac{72}{x^3} \right\rvert \le \tfrac{1}{192}​x372​​≤1921​, which together stay below 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​. So the bracket sits between −32-\tfrac{3}{2}−23​ and −12-\tfrac{1}{2}−21​ and is certainly negative, and fff has the opposite sign to x3x^3x3 out there: large and positive on the far left, large and negative on the far right. No limits are needed, only the stated threshold.

    Part C

    The verdict is decided by the multiplicity of each root, not by the fact that it is a root.

    At x=−6x = -6x=−6. Group the factor as (x+6)2(x + 6)^2(x+6)2, a square, so it is positive for every x≠−6x \ne -6x=−6 and contributes the same +++ on both sides. Part A found f>0f > 0f>0 on both x<−6x < -6x<−6 and −6<x<2-6 < x < 2−6<x<2, which is that fact in the sign chart: no sign change, so the graph touches the axis at (−6,0)(-6, 0)(−6,0) and turns back.

    At x=2x = 2x=2. The factor (2−x)(2 - x)(2−x) has power 111, an odd power, so it carries its own sign:

    2−x>0 for x<2,2−x<0 for x>22 - x > 0 \text{ for } x < 2, \qquad 2 - x < 0 \text{ for } x > 22−x>0 for x<2,2−x<0 for x>2

    The sign of fff therefore flips across 222, and the graph crosses the axis there. Neither verdict looked at a curve; both came from the powers.

Expanded, f(x)=−x3−10x2−12x+72=x3(−1−10x−12x2+72x3)f(x) = -x^3 - 10x^2 - 12x + 72 = x^3\left(-1 - \tfrac{10}{x} - \tfrac{12}{x^2} + \tfrac{72}{x^3}\right)f(x)=−x3−10x2−12x+72=x3(−1−x10​−x212​+x372​), whose bracket is negative once ∣x∣≥24\lvert x \rvert \ge 24∣x∣≥24, so the graph rises on the far left and falls on the far right. The squared factor makes the graph touch and turn back at −6-6−6; the power 111 makes it cross at 222.

    The answer

    Part A

    The excluded inputs are x=−2x = -2x=−2 and x=−3x = -3x=−3. The missing point is (−2,4)(-2, 4)(−2,4).

    Part B

    x2x+3\dfrac{x^2}{x + 3}x+3x2​, on the inputs fff allows. At x=−3x = -3x=−3 the offending factor does not cancel, so the graph runs off along the vertical line x=−3x = -3x=−3 instead of losing a single point.

    Part C

    They are not the same function. Their values agree wherever both are defined, but −2-2−2 lies in ggg's natural domain and not in fff's, so the equal-domains condition fails. Declaring ggg on the inputs x≠−3x \ne -3x=−3 and x≠−2x \ne -2x=−2 repairs it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Factor both parts. The denominator decides the domain.

    f(x)=x2(x+2)(x+2)(x+3)f(x) = \frac{x^2(x + 2)}{(x + 2)(x + 3)}f(x)=(x+2)(x+3)x2(x+2)​

    The denominator vanishes at x=−2x = -2x=−2 and at x=−3x = -3x=−3, so both are excluded. For every other input the shared factor cancels, leaving x2x+3\tfrac{x^2}{x + 3}x+3x2​.     Cancelling the shared factor gives the agreeing rule, valid at every input fff accepts.

    The answer

    Part A

    2x+8=2(x+4)2x + 8 = 2(x + 4)2x+8=2(x+4), so b=2b = 2b=2, h=−4h = -4h=−4, a=−12a = -\tfrac{1}{2}a=−21​ and k=3k = 3k=3: compress horizontally by 222, shift left 444, halve each height and reflect it, then shift up 333.

    Part B

    Domain −6≤x≤3-6 \le x \le 3−6≤x≤3 and range 0≤y≤40 \le y \le 40≤y≤4. The old top 666 became the new bottom 000, and the old bottom −2-2−2 became the new top 444.

    Part C

    The inside acts on the number handed to fff, so finding where a point lands means solving the inside for xxx, which touches the input alone; the outside acts on the height fff has already returned. Solving is also why the factor comes out first: it divides the shift, making the move left 444 rather than left 888.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Pull the input multiplier out of the inside before reading anything, and read the outside straight off.

    2x+8=2(x+4)⟹b=2, h=−4,a=−12, k=32x + 8 = 2(x + 4) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad b = 2,\ h = -4, \qquad a = -\tfrac{1}{2},\ k = 32x+8=2(x+4)⟹b=2, h=−4,a=−21​, k=3

    On the inside, b=2b = 2b=2 divides every input by 222, a horizontal compression by 222, and h=−4h = -4h=−4 shifts by −4-4−4, that is left 444. On the outside, a=−12a = -\tfrac{1}{2}a=−21​ halves every height and flips its sign, and k=3k = 3k=3 then raises the result by 333. Read the +8+8+8 without factoring and the shift comes out as 888, which is four times too far.

    Part B

    The two halves never mix: the inside pair moves the domain and the outside pair moves the range. A point (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) lands at (ub+h, av+k)\left(\tfrac{u}{b} + h,\ av + k\right)(bu​+h, av+k), so send each endpoint through the matching half.

    −4↦−42−4=−6,14↦142−4=3,−2↦−12(−2)+3=4,6↦−12(6)+3=0-4 \mapsto \tfrac{-4}{2} - 4 = -6, \quad 14 \mapsto \tfrac{14}{2} - 4 = 3, \qquad -2 \mapsto -\tfrac{1}{2}(-2) + 3 = 4, \quad 6 \mapsto -\tfrac{1}{2}(6) + 3 = 0−4↦2−4​−4=−6,14↦214​−4=3,−2↦−21​(−2)+3=4,6↦−21​(6)+3=0

    The domain endpoints keep their order, since b=2b = 2b=2 is positive. The range endpoints swap, since a=−12a = -\tfrac{1}{2}a=−21​ is negative, so the interval has to be reported from the smaller value up: 0≤y≤40 \le y \le 40≤y≤4.

    Part C

    Why the halves do not mix. A point (u,v)(u, v)(u,v) on fff reappears at the input xxx where the number handed to fff equals uuu, and at the height obtained by putting vvv through the outside arithmetic. The first is an equation in xxx alone and the second a computation on vvv alone:

    b(x−h)=u ⟹ x=ub+h,y=av+kb(x - h) = u \ \Longrightarrow\ x = \frac{u}{b} + h, \qquad y = av + kb(x−h)=u ⟹ x=bu​+h,y=av+k

    Neither expression contains the other's variable, so an inside change can never move a height and an outside change can never move an input.

    Why the factoring comes first. Solving undoes the inside operations in reverse order, dividing by bbb before adding hhh. That is exactly what the factored form displays. Left unfactored, the +8+8+8 looks like the whole shift, but the division by b=2b = 2b=2 reaches it too:

    2x+8=u ⟹ x=u2−42x + 8 = u \ \Longrightarrow\ x = \frac{u}{2} - 42x+8=u ⟹ x=2u​−4

    The shift is −4-4−4, a move left 444, not left 888.

    In one line

    The inside factors as 2(x+4)2(x + 4)2(x+4), so the moves are a horizontal compression by 222, a shift left 444, a halving of every height with a reflection, and a shift up 333. The transformed graph has domain −6≤x≤3-6 \le x \le 3−6≤x≤3 and range 0≤y≤40 \le y \le 40≤y≤4, with the old top 666 arriving at the new bottom 000. The inside reaches only the input because finding a landing input means solving the inside for xxx, and that same solving divides the shift, making it left 444 rather than left 888.

    One direction. Feed xxx through fff and then through the candidate:

    f−1(f(x))=5+12−(12−(x−5)2)=5+(x−5)2=5+∣x−5∣f^{-1}\big(f(x)\big) = 5 + \sqrt{12 - \big(12 - (x - 5)^2\big)} = 5 + \sqrt{(x - 5)^2} = 5 + \lvert x - 5 \rvertf−1(f(x))=5+12−(12−(x−5)2)​=5+(x−5)2​=5+∣x−5∣

    The other direction. Feed xxx through the candidate and then through fff:

    The check the classmate ran is genuine: for x≤12x \le 12x≤12,

    f(g(x))=12−(5−12−x−5)2=12−(12−x)=x.f\big(g(x)\big) = 12 - \big(5 - \sqrt{12 - x} - 5\big)^2 = 12 - (12 - x) = x.f(g(x))=12−(5−12−x​−5)2=12−(12−x)=x.

    But an inverse has to undo fff from both directions, so run the other order on the unrestricted fff:

The input x=9x = 9x=9 settles it: f(9)=12−16=−4f(9) = 12 - 16 = -4f(9)=12−16=−4, and g(−4)=5−16=1g(-4) = 5 - \sqrt{16} = 1g(−4)=5−16​=1, which is not 999. That is the labour symmetry saves: one half of the graph is proved from the other.

    The parity of the exponents in the expanded rule and the multiplicity of a root are two different things, and the claim confuses them. Build a polynomial that has only odd powers and still carries an even-power factor.

    Part B

    g(x)=x2g(x) = \tfrac{x}{2}g(x)=2x​ on x≤2x \le 2x≤2, and g(x)=x−6g(x) = x - 6g(x)=x−6 on x>7x > 7x>7. No number is claimed by both cases, and none between 222 and 777 is claimed at all.

    As declared it has none. Any candidate ggg would need f(g(5))=5f(g(5)) = 5f(g(5))=5, and 555 is not a value fff ever produces, so f∘gf \circ gf∘g cannot be the identity on the declared codomain. Declaring the codomain to be the set of values produced repairs it, leaving one-to-oneness as the only thing left to check.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The cases are disjoint and cover every real number, so fff is a genuine function; take the values one case at a time.

    x≤1 ⟹ 2x≤2,x>1 ⟹ x+6>7x \le 1 \ \Longrightarrow\ 2x \le 2, \qquad x > 1 \ \Longrightarrow\ x + 6 > 7x≤1 ⟹ 2x≤2,x>1 ⟹ x+6>7

    Each case is a line, so it produces every value in its own interval and nothing beyond it. Together they produce all of y≤2y \le 2y≤2 and all of y>7y > 7y>7, and the boundary 222 is attained at x=1x = 1x=1 while 777 is only approached, since x>1x > 1x>1 is strict. So the values with 2<y≤72 < y \le 72<y≤7 are never output: the range has a gap, even though the domain has none.

    Part B

    Each case of fff is one-to-one on its own piece, and the two pieces produce sets with no number in common, so no output is ever reached twice and fff is one-to-one overall. Undo each case on the values that case produces.

    y=2x (x≤1) ⟹ x=y2 (y≤2),y=x+6 (x>1) ⟹ x=y−6 (y>7)y = 2x \ (x \le 1) \ \Longrightarrow\ x = \frac{y}{2} \ (y \le 2), \qquad y = x + 6 \ (x > 1) \ \Longrightarrow\ x = y - 6 \ (y > 7)y=2x (x≤1) ⟹ x=2y​ (y≤2),y=x+6 (x>1) ⟹ x=y−6 (y>7)

    Call that rule ggg, holding the name f−1f^{-1}f−1 back until the declaration has been settled. It is itself a rule in two cases, with domain exactly the set part A found. Checking one value each way: f(1)=2f(1) = 2f(1)=2 and g(2)=1g(2) = 1g(2)=1; f(4)=10f(4) = 10f(4)=10 and g(10)=4g(10) = 4g(10)=4.

    Part C

    One-to-oneness is not the whole condition when the codomain is declared larger than the set of values produced, and here it is.

    Which composition fails. Suppose ggg were a two-sided inverse. Then f∘gf \circ gf∘g would have to be the identity on the whole declared codomain, so f(g(y))=yf(g(y)) = yf(g(y))=y for every real yyy. But f(g(y))f(g(y))f(g(y)) is a genuine output of fff, and part A showed fff never outputs anything strictly between 222 and 777:

    f(g(5))=5 is impossible, since 5 is not a value f produces.f\big(g(5)\big) = 5 \ \text{is impossible, since } 5 \ \text{is not a value } f \ \text{produces.}f(g(5))=5 is impossible, since 5 is not a value f produces.

    So f∘g=id⁡f \circ g = \operatorname{id}f∘g=id fails, at 555 and at every value in the gap. The other composition is fine: g∘f=id⁡g \circ f = \operatorname{id}g∘f=id holds for the rule of part B, because fff is one-to-one.

    The repair. Nothing is wrong with the rule, so nothing about the rule needs changing. What was wrong was the declaration: shrink the codomain to the set of values fff actually produces, every y≤2y \le 2y≤2 together with every y>7y > 7y>7. With the codomain taken as the range, reaching every declared value is automatic, and one-to-oneness is then the only condition to check, which part B verified; only at that point does the rule of part B earn the name f−1f^{-1}f−1. This is why the clean statement 'invertible exactly when one-to-one' carries a hypothesis about the codomain; with a larger codomain the condition is one-to-one and onto.

    In one line

    The rule produces every y≤2y \le 2y≤2 and every y>7y > 7y>7, and never a value with 2<y≤72 < y \le 72<y≤7. Its undoing rule is g(x)=x2g(x) = \tfrac{x}{2}g(x)=2x​ on x≤2x \le 2x≤2 and x−6x - 6x−6 on x>7x > 7x>7. With the codomain declared to be all real numbers there is no two-sided inverse, since f∘gf \circ gf∘g would have to return values such as 555 that fff never produces; declaring the codomain to be the set of produced values repairs it, and one-to-oneness is then all that remains to check.

Marking rubrics

Work every question first. Then mark your own paper against these, giving yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down.

1. One curve, and a question that waits on a declaration 9 points

Part A 3

  • Solves the relation for yyy and keeps both signs the square root carries. 2
  • Reports how many outputs each declaration produces at the stated input, naming which declaration each count belongs to. 1

Part B 3

  • Exhibits two inputs with a shared output and argues from them to the verdict on one-to-oneness. 2
  • Connects the shared output to the failure of the reading with xxx as the input, through the swap of coordinates. 1

Part C 3

  • Grants that the set of points is fixed, then locates the verdict in the pairing of that set with a declared input. 2
  • Names the two line tests as the same test asked about the two different readings. 1

2. The slot, the quotient, and the one input the cancelling costs 10 points

Part A 4

  • Substitutes the whole expression x+hx + hx+h into the slot and combines the two fractions over a common denominator. 2
  • Cancels the factor of hhh and records all three restrictions the simplified fraction carries. 2

Part B 3

  • Evaluates the simplified expression and the direct difference quotient, and sets the two results side by side. 2
  • States what the number measures for this rule, as a change in output per unit of input across the step. 1

Part C 3

  • Grants the agreement on the overlap and then appeals to the domain, not the values, as what settles equality. 2
  • Names h=0h = 0h=0 as the disagreeing input and traces it to the division that produced the simplified form. 1

3. Everything the factored form already knows 11 points

Part A 3

  • Reads both zeros off the factors and uses them to cut the line into the intervals to be tested. 1
  • Gives each factor a fixed sign on each interval and multiplies those signs to reach the sign of fff there. 2

Part B 4

  • Expands the product and factors out the highest power of xxx to isolate a bracket of correction terms. 2
  • Bounds the correction terms beyond a stated threshold and reads the behaviour of both ends from the sign of the leading power. 2

Part C 4

  • Argues that an even power holds one sign on both sides of its root, so the graph meets the axis there and turns back. 2
  • Argues that an odd power carries the sign of its single factor, so the sign flips and the graph crosses. 2

4. Two excluded inputs, only one of which leaves a gap 11 points

Part A 4

  • Factors the denominator and names both inputs it rejects, before any cancelling is done. 2
  • Identifies which excluded input leaves a single missing point and reads its height off the simplified rule. 2

Part B 3

  • Cancels only the factor the numerator and denominator share, and keeps the excluded input attached to the simplified rule. 2
  • Says what happens at the excluded input whose factor survives, distinguishing it from a single missing point. 1

Part C 4

  • Tests all three conditions of function equality and identifies the one that fails. 2
  • Exhibits an input that lies in one domain and not the other, with the value one rule gives there. 1
  • States a declared domain for ggg under which all three conditions hold, leaving both rules untouched. 1

5. Four numbers, and the coordinate each one is allowed to touch 12 points

Part A 4

  • Factors the inside into the form b(x−h)b(x - h)b(x−h) before naming any shift. 2
  • Names all four moves with their exact amounts and directions, keeping the inside pair separate from the outside pair. 2

Part B 4

  • Sends the domain endpoints through the inside pair only and the range endpoints through the outside pair only. 2
  • Reports each interval from its smaller value up and names which old endpoint became which new one. 2

Part C 4

  • Argues that finding a new input means solving the inside for xxx, so the inside numbers reach the first coordinate only. 2
  • Argues that the outside acts on a height already produced, so it reaches the second coordinate only. 1
  • Ties the factoring step to the fact that the input multiplier divides the shift, and states the amount the unfactored reading would give. 1

6. What survives two stages, and what a superscript is counting 12 points

Part A 4

  • Substitutes the rule of the inner function into the input slot of the outer one and simplifies. 1
  • Imposes both conditions, the inner function's own requirement and the requirement on its output, and names which excluded input each produces. 3

Part B 4

  • Computes the composition by substituting the whole first output back into the rule. 2
  • Computes the square of the output separately and gives an input at which the two results differ. 2

Part C 4

  • Builds the composite and states both conditions, the one on the inner input and the one on the inner output. 2
  • Produces one input inside the domain and one outside it, with the value of the inner rule at each as the reason. 2

7. Undoing a rule, and the checks that decide it 14 points

Part A 4

  • Solves for the input and chooses the sign of the root that the restriction forces. 2
  • Gives the inverse's domain as the set of values the restricted rule produces, not as the original domain. 2

Part B 5

  • Carries out both compositions rather than one, each on its own domain. 2
  • Treats the square root of a square as an absolute value and says what the restriction does to it. 2
  • Names the restriction each direction depends on, and what would fail without it. 1

Part C 5

  • Computes the composition the classmate did not run, on the unrestricted domain. 2
  • Names one input at which that composition fails to return its own value, with the two intermediate values. 1
  • Argues that a two-sided requirement is what the failure is about, rather than an arithmetic slip in the classmate's check. 2

8. A quintic taken apart factor by factor 12 points

Part A 3

  • Removes the common factor and factors the remaining quartic as a quadratic in x2x^2x2. 2
  • Lists all five zeros, each read from its own linear factor. 1

Part B 5

  • Notes that the domain holds −x-x−x whenever it holds xxx, then computes f(−x)f(-x)f(−x) and compares it with −f(x)-f(x)−f(x). 2
  • Assigns each factor a fixed sign on the stated interval and multiplies them. 1
  • Transfers the sign to the reflected interval using the odd identity rather than by recomputing the factor signs there. 2

Part C 4

  • Produces a polynomial whose expanded form carries only odd powers and whose factored form carries an even power. 2
  • Identifies the root at which the graph turns back and ties the verdict to the even power on its factor. 2

9. Two input maps, two orders, one measurable gap 14 points

Part A 4

  • Builds each order by tracking where an input lands, rather than by reading the moves off a finished formula. 2
  • Gives both insides in factored and expanded form, with the shift in each matching its own order. 2

Part B 4

  • Applies the landing rule under both orders and leaves the height untouched, since neither move acts on the output. 2
  • Gives the horizontal separation of the two landings and says that it is the same for every point of the graph. 2

Part C 6

  • Writes both orders as landing maps in the letters bbb and hhh, with the compression dividing the shift in exactly one of them. 2
  • Shows the difference of the two landings carries no input variable, and concludes from that alone that the graphs are a translation apart. 2
  • States the translation in terms of bbb and hhh and gives both conditions under which it is zero. 2

10. A rule that never returns certain numbers 14 points

Part A 4

  • Works out the values each case produces, keeping the boundary input with the case whose condition it satisfies. 2
  • Reports the gap between the two sets, open at the attained end and closed at the approached one. 2

Part B 4

  • Undoes each case separately and attaches it to the values that case produces rather than to the original inputs. 2
  • Notes that the two cases of the inverse share no input, which is what makes the rule single-valued. 2

Part C 6

  • Names which of the two compositions cannot be the identity on the declared codomain, and why the other one is unaffected. 2
  • Exhibits one value of the declared codomain that no input reaches, and argues from it that no candidate can succeed. 2
  • States the change to the declaration that repairs it, and says what condition is then left to check. 2
